questions.question: Explain why informal settlements grow in South African cities and describe the risks that residents face.
questions.expected_answer: When people arrive faster than formal housing can be built, they rent backyard rooms, crowd into existing homes, occupy buildings or build their own shelters in informal settlements. These often grow on empty but unsuitable land such as flood plains, steep slopes, land under power lines or beside railways and highways, old dumps and wetlands, with shelters of corrugated iron, wood and plastic, small irregular plots and few roads so emergency vehicles cannot enter. Shack fires spread quickly because shelters are close and flammable and people use paraffin, candles and open fires, as in Imizamo Yethu in 2017; flooding is dangerous, as in the KwaZulu-Natal floods of April 2022 that killed more than 400 people; and residents without secure tenure may be evicted. Despite millions of subsidised houses since 1994, the backlog remains large because cities keep growing and households keep forming.

questions.question: Describe the problems of providing water, sanitation, electricity and refuse removal in rapidly growing cities and explain why services fall behind.
questions.expected_answer: In many informal settlements people collect water from shared standpipes, with long queues and walks mainly by women and children and risk of contamination, and South Africa's water scarcity adds pressure, as in Cape Town's near Day Zero during the 2015 to 2018 drought. Sanitation may be shared chemical toilets, pit latrines or none, spreading diarrhoea and cholera, creating safety risks at night, and overloaded sewers pollute rivers and beaches. Many settlements lack legal electricity, so people use paraffin, candles, wood and gas, causing fires and indoor smoke, or make dangerous illegal connections, while national supply has faced load shedding. Uncollected refuse attracts rats and flies and blocks drains. Services fall behind because municipalities need money, skilled staff, planning and time; dense irregular layouts make infrastructure hard to fit; some land is unsafe or not municipal; and municipalities face financial and management problems, leading to service delivery protests.

questions.question: Describe how rapid urban growth affects health care and education, and evaluate responses.
questions.expected_answer: Crowding, poor sanitation, unsafe water and indoor smoke spread disease, including tuberculosis, of which South Africa has one of the highest rates, HIV, diarrhoeal diseases in young children and respiratory illness, with injuries from fires, violence and road accidents. Clinics are overcrowded with long queues and staff and medicine shortages, often far from new settlements, and private care is unaffordable for most. Schools become overcrowded, with large classes and too few classrooms, desks and textbooks; some settlements have no nearby school; and learners struggle to study because of crowding, noise, no light and water collection, while suburban schools are better resourced. Responses include new clinics, mobile clinics, community health workers, hygiene and vaccination campaigns, new schools and mobile classrooms, scholar transport, school nutrition programmes and no-fee schools; they help, but must keep pace with growth, and improving housing and services also improves health and education because the issues are linked.
